claims.text: Increasing chromium content promotes formation of a continuous, protective chromium-rich oxide layer.
The chromium-rich oxide layer is the primary mechanism responsible for corrosion resistance in steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications.
The standard steel currently used in these applications has a characteristic baseline chromium level and typical microstructure.
Chromium content will be increased while other alloying elements and processing conditions are held unchanged.
Baseline and chromium-enhanced steels will be exposed to identical controlled corrosive environments.
High-temperature acidic or chloride-containing media are representative of chemical-processing and nuclear-service conditions.
The relevant structural mediator is a continuous and intact chromium-rich Cr2O3 passive film on the steel surface.
Added chromium preferentially oxidizes to form Cr2O3.
The resulting Cr2O3 layer is stable and adherent.
A stable, adherent Cr2O3 layer reduces active dissolution at the steel surface.
A stable, adherent Cr2O3 layer reduces ion transport at the steel surface.
Reduced active dissolution and ion transport lower the corrosion rate.
Chromium-enhanced steel will have a lower corrosion rate than the baseline steel under identical conditions.
Chromium-enhanced steel will develop a thicker chromium-rich oxide film than the baseline steel.
Chromium-enhanced steel will develop a more continuous chromium-rich oxide film than the baseline steel.
The hypothesis is expected to apply under service-like chemical-processing and nuclear-power conditions within controlled temperature, pressure, and solution-composition ranges.
The corrosion-rate reduction may depend on the magnitude of chromium addition and the corrosive environment.
Minor alloying elements may affect the proposed relationship.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant corrosion-rate reduction or a noticeably thicker and more continuous chromium-rich film would falsify the proposed primary-film mechanism.
